CANOE 

TRIP 

COUNSELLORS: 

TAKE NOTE! 

-•- 

Walter D. Mingle , 

Director of Canoe Trips, 

Camp Nominingue, Que. 


At Camp Nominingue every coun¬ 
sellor and Junior counsellor is a Trip 
Counsellor. Most counsellors will take 
out two canoe trips from three to 
eight days in length, during a season. 
We send out parties of two counsellors 
and five campers in two canoes, pair¬ 
ing up a new counsellor with one who 
has had previous canoe trip experi¬ 
ence. 

During the advance party and dur¬ 
ing the first few days of camp each 
season, we have an in-service training 
program for counsellors. Part of this 
time is spent in preparing counsellors 
to take out canoe trips. We realize 
that the experience gained on a 
canoe trip is invaluable and with 
each trip the counsellor becomes a 
better trip leader. However, we feel 
we would be remiss in our duty if we 
failed to expose the newcomers to the 
experience gained in previous years. 

To do this we have several theoreti¬ 
cal and practical sessions. The practi¬ 
cal sessions deal with CANOEING 
SKILLS; PORTAGING; GAMP- 
CRAFT SKILLS (axemanship, tent 
pitching, etc.); COOKING and 
ARTIFICIAL RESPIRATION. Each 
trip Leader is provided with the fol¬ 
lowing mimeographed material: a 
menu, a food list, cooking and mixing 
directions, an equipment list, a check 
list of things to be done before de¬ 
parting, a map, a portage report 
covering his area, and a trip report 
check list to be completed upon his 
return. 

The lecture part of the In-Service 
Training deals with the following 
points, which arc listed here in 
brief: 


Planning the Trip: 

1. Discuss the trip together as a party 


10 


Canadian Camping 



and decide the destination, the route 
and some purpose or project for the 
trip, such as collecting driftwood, 
making a campsite or visiting some 
popular spot. 

2. Make sure everyone knows the 
route—where you plan to camp each 
night, where you plan to eat lunch 
each day, how many miles of portag¬ 
ing, how many miles of paddling each 
day. These plans may be modified 
daily in the light of existing circum¬ 
stances, but everyone should know the 
overall picture. 

3. Always check off your food and 
equipment against the prepared list to 
make sure you have not forgotten 
anyhing. Similarly, check your depar¬ 
ture check list. 

4. Find out the abilities of the mem¬ 
bers of your party. Who can use an 
axe well, who likes to cook, who are 
the better paddlers, what is their 
swimming ability. 

5. Make sure you know the date and 
time of your departure and return. 
Leave this information and an itiner¬ 
ary of your route at camp, as well as 
an accurate list of the members of 
your party. 


Travelling: 

1. Travel as a party. Balance the 
paddling ability between the canoes so 
that they will stay together without 
one group having to overwork. 

2. When portaging stay together. Bal¬ 
ance the load so that the strongest 
camper carries the heaviest load, and 
the smallest camper has no more than 
he is able to cope with. The lead per¬ 
son should be instructed to stop if the 


Toronto , Canada, December 1959 


trail forks or he cannot see or hear 
the rest of the party. 

3. Plan your route across each lake, 
taking advantage of the wind and the 
shelter of the shore, if need be. 

4. Do not attempt to cross a lake if 
there is any doubt that the weakest 
member of your party cannot make 
it. Safety first. WATCH FOR WEA¬ 
THER SIGNS. Do not try to cross a 
lake if there may be a storm coming 
up. Skirt the shore, or stay where you 
are until you are sure your party can 
make it. 

5. Have an organized plan for getting 
people out of the canoes at portages 
and in again at the next lake. Try to 
do these things efficiently and as 
quickly as possible. 


At the Campsite: 

1. Organize the setting up of camp. 
Assign duties. Attempt to do all the 
jobs as efficiently as possible. Remem¬ 
ber, as a counsellor you are supposed 
to be teaching campers the best way 
of doing things. 

2. Discuss the forthcoming meal with 
your party—they are very interested. 
Have a schedule of work so that all 
campers get an opportunity to help 
with the cooking and campcraft. 
Follow the menu. Organize your kit¬ 
chen, plan the order of the meal’s 
preparation, and take pride in pre¬ 
paring meals quickly. 

3. Always pitch your tent, make a 
latrine, a garbage pit (not in the lake 
please), a fireplace, and a kitchen 
table. 

continued on page 26

CAMPING 


By Mrs. George Brigden, R.N., B.Sc.N. 


On the opening day of Camp, and 
again in August, the children who 
arrive at camp should be sent directly 
to the infirmary, even before they 
collect their baggage or go to their 
cabins. Any health certificates which 
have not been mailed in a few days 
prior to Camp could be presented by 
the child or the counsellor, as the 
camper takes his turn in line for his 
medical examination. 

Every camp ought to have a regis¬ 
tered nurse on the Staff, and if the 
camp is large, a doctor, and a nurse’s 
assistant, or better still, another nurse 
in attendance. On these days when 
the new campers arrive, it is advisable, 
in the small camp, to call in the local 
doctor to give the campers their physi¬ 
cal examination. Camp nurses and 
directors should never be satisfied with 
the report of the examination done by 
the city doctor, for it is possible for 
the child to contact some contageous 
disease in the intervening time between 
his last check-up and his arrival at 
Camp. Careful watch, therefore should 
be made for such skin diseases as ath¬ 
lete’s foot and impetago, and for the 
communicable diseases, chickenpox, 
measles etc. 

Either that day or the next, as 
soon as the children have unpacked, 
the nurse, during a rest hour period, 
would be well advised to go from 
cabin to cabin and collect any medi¬ 
cine which the children and coun¬ 
sellors have brought with them. Some 
children will bring their drugs direct¬ 
ly to the infirmary, but many are 


tardy or forget altogether. It is im¬ 
portant, especially with counsellors, 
to ask for their cosmetic alchohol, 
aspirins, laxatives and other common 
types of drugs, which are not harmful 
to the owner, but which should not 
be accessible to the younger age 
groups, for fear of overdose. All drugs 
and medicines should be kept in the 
infirmary, and dispensed as ordered 
or as required. This is a very important 
health rule to observe. 

Drugs to be taken with meals 
ought never to be left in the dining 
room. The nurse, coming to lunch, 
can bring them with her in a little 
box, and keep them at her table. This 
has a dual purpose. First, the nurse 
knows that the child is taking the 
medicine, and second, the nurse can 
order more when the supply nears ex¬ 
haustion. I do not feel that the 
supervision of the taking of medicines 
with meals, should ever be the coun¬ 
sellors’ responsibility. 

During the summer, many camps 
make it a point to have medical re¬ 
presentation at each weekly staff 
meeting. Either the nurse or doctor 
presents a weekly report on any of 
the general conditions in camp (from 
a health standpoint) which may be 
altered or improved. Problems may 
range from the sanitary conditions in 
the dining room, poor health habits in 
cabins, to the ideal length of time for 
the swimming period on cool days. 
Counsellors may seek advice concern¬ 
ing the health of campers in their 
charge, and health talks are often in- 


12 


Canadian Camping 




. . • • from the NURSE'S VIEWPOINT 

Our readers who plan to attend the Ontario Camping Association conference in Toronto 
on March 25th and 26th, 1960, at the King Edward Hotel, will be pleased to know that 
Mrs. Brigden is to conduct a session on the subject of health at camp. 


itiated in this way. This practice of 
instituting medical reports at weekly 
staff meetings is highly recommended, 
and could be successfully adopted in 
all camps. 

Some infirmaries are quite elaborate, 
and any nurse who has a large variety 
of equipment at her disposal, is in¬ 
deed fortunate. Whether or not this 
is the case in your camp, I should like 
to stress a few essential items which 
every health centre should contain. 

Keep a small locked cupboard or 
strongbox in your infirmary for 
drugs, such as barbiturates or poison¬ 
ous medicines which are too danger¬ 
ous to leave in an open cupboard. 

Some drugs, such as allergy and 
anti-tetanus serums have to be kept 
on ice. The kitchen refrigerator is 
not the place for them. If the camp 
can purchase an icebox, this is ideal, 
for then both drugs and cold drinks 
and jellys can be kept at a desirable 
temperature. A good substitute for the 
icebox is the lined tin box which, 
though too small for the storage of 
foods, is large enough to accommo¬ 
date drugs. 

An isolation unit ought to be a 
“must”. I do not mean by this, a 
separate room set aside for conta- 
geous diseases only, but I am referr¬ 
ing to a complete unit of articles 
used for complete nursing care. A 
child with mumps, for instance, needs 
her own bedside table, her own basin, 
cup, soapdish, dishes and tray, and 
these should never be mixed with 


other equipment. An infirmary with 
two or three beds and only one hand 
basin, to cite an example, is not 
properly equipped. If a child has 
mumps in one room, and another 
child lies in bed next door with an 
upset stomach, one basin cannot be 
shared by both children. 

Every camp nurse requires facilities 
for sterilizing supplies, and any small 
stove and covered receptacle should be 
adequate. 

A final word about equipment. If 
you do not already have it, put a 
stove in your health centre to pro¬ 
vide warmth on cold and damp days. 
Head colds and respiratory infections 
are the commonest complaints in 
every camp. You will speed your 
camper’s health back to normal if you 
can provide warm dry air in your 
infirmary. 

Fatigue in Camp and 

Some Ways to Prevent It 

In order to combat fatigue among 
campers, pre-camp education for staff 
members is an ideal way to begin. At 
the spring meeting, the camp nurse, 
or doctor, or director, is well advised 
to emphasize to the staff, the im¬ 
portance of plenty of rest for each 
camper. All campers are experienc¬ 
ing a growing period, and counsellors, 
appreciating this, can more readily 
perceive the importance of adequate 
rest and sleep, and a balanced activity 
program. They can learn to watch for 
signs of fatigue in their campers, and 
gear the cabin program accordingly, 
turn to next page 


Toronto, Canada , December 1959 


13 


or bring their problems to the atten¬ 
tion of senior staff members. 

The first couple of days at camp 
are an exciting time for any child, as 
he or she is busy adjusting to new 
surroundings, new people, and even 
perhaps, new food. If the program is 
planned to provide for plenty of free 
periods in which to unpack and ex¬ 
plore, the camper will make a heal¬ 
thier beginning. 

Swimming periods ought to be very 
short at first. New sets of muscles are 
being brought into play, and a fifteen 
minute swim in the morning and in 
the afternoon is adequate. This 
general rule can be applied to every 
new sport, of course, but need not be 
so strongly emphasized. 

Throughout the summer, the daily 
afternoon rest should always be ob¬ 
served. The question has often been 
raised, “HOW STRICTLY?” After 
the noon meal, campers and coun¬ 
sellors can go directly to their cabins. 
This is not the time for tuck, (that 
can be fitted into the daily pro¬ 
gramme quite successfully after the 
supper hour). 

Counsellors often find the rest 
period the only free time in which to 
attend short staff meetings, but at 
least one staff member should be in 
each cabin. Rest patrol is as impor¬ 
tant as night patrol, and campers 
should stay on their beds for at least 
an hour, depending on the age group. 
Reading books and writing letters are 
excellent silent occupations, but talk¬ 
ing should be forbidden except in 
cases of necessity, and sleep habits en¬ 
couraged. Setting an early bedtime 
hour is an excellent remedy for the 
noisy group. 

The evening program can be so 
organized that the last ten or fifteen 
minutes are toned down in intensity. 


Some camps plan quiet firesides with 
evening songs, a story or some form of 
worship. This helps to prepare the 
campers for bedtime, and they will go 
quietly to their cabins after “taps” 
and not finish the day tense and ex¬ 
cited from a stimulating programme. 
Again, a certain amount of discipline 
is necessary in order to get the camp 
to sleep. Where a large number of 
campers are involved, it is essential to 
be very firm about this, or chaos will 
surely ensue. 

The success of the afternoon nap 
and observance of bedtime rules, how¬ 
ever, depend largely on the pattern 
set the first days of camp, and the 
attitude of counsellors toward their 
cabin groups. Children soon realize 
that rules arc not meant to be broken, 
and with a little firmness on the part 
of everyone at the outset, campers 
soon adjust to the routine, and appre¬ 
ciate the maximum of rest and sleep. 

One final word regarding fatigue. 
No two people are the same in physi¬ 
cal build or emotional structure. All 
staff members, especially cabin coun¬ 
sellors need to watch for signs of 
fatigue in the individual child. Camp 
life is strenuous and some campers 
need a periodic rest from the full 
daily program. Often a night spent in 
the infirmary is all that the child re¬ 
quires to regain lost vitality. Some¬ 
times such enervating sports as rid¬ 
ing or basketball can be temporarily 
replaced by a “free” period, or the 
hour spent at handicrafts instead. 
Every situation differs from every 
other, and should be dealt with in¬ 
dividually, according to the degree 
and nature of the fatigue experienced 
by the camper. 

Every child is at camp to have a 
holiday. He or she has had a long, 
hard year at school, and requires a 
programme designed to build him or 


14 


Canadian Camping 



her up for the winter months. If the 
camper returns to the city at the end 
of the holiday very much in need of 
a rest, one of the main purposes of 
camp has been defeated. Let each 
camper participate in activities at his 
or her own pace. Each will be a 
healthier, happier person. 

Guard the Health of Your 
Canoe Trippers 

Canoe trips are experiences to be 
enjoyed. The object of any trip is 
never to see how much paddling can 
be done in a set space of time, or how 
many portages can be crossed, but is 
designed instead, to afford pleasure to 
the camper, to help him gain experi¬ 
ence in woodlore, and to provide an 
opportunity for campers to live and 
work in harmony together. No child 
should come back from a canoe trip 
physically exhausted and emotionally 
unstrung. 

The day before a camper or coun¬ 
sellor sets out on a canoe trip, he or 
she needs a medical check-up, and the 
reminder to go to bed early that 
night. In the morning, when equip¬ 
ment is being packed, and canoes 
loaded, a counsellor, or some other 
authorized staff member can check the 
clothing and bedding of each camper, 
to insure that the child has proper 
protection against sun, rain and cold. 

Plan to have the initial trips of the 
season short overnight excursions, or 
three day trips for older campers. 
The pace should be stimulating, at an 
even tempo, but never pressing. Trip¬ 
pers should select a camp site about 
4 p.m. and begin to make camp. To 
paddle until 5 or 6 o’clock is both too 
late and too long. A late stop means 
a late supper, a late camp fire, and a 
late bedtime. Every canoe trip should 
carry one tent in case of rain, and the 
ideal time to pitch it is before supper 


. Toronto, Canada , December 1959 


every afternoon, not after the rain has 
started and the bedding is damp. 

The short route with the side trips 
is best, if this is possible. This way, 
trippers can see a great deal of coun¬ 
try without becoming over-tired, as 
they can plan excursions to fit their 
timetable, and still be close to the 
main camp. This is suggested because 
campers on the round-trip route often 
encounter bad weather, and are ham¬ 
pered from travelling and consequent¬ 
ly are forced to paddle furiously the 
last day or two, in order to arrive 
home on schedule. 

Often, on canoe trips, the same 
camp site is used over and over again 
throughout the season. If this is the 
case, some kind of lavatory ought to 
be erected, which can easily be kept 
clean and sanitary by each group of 
campers. This is very important, and 
not only can water pollution be pre¬ 
vented, but pleasant surroundings can 
thereafter be maintained for trippers, 
and for any cottagers living in the 
area. 

All good trippers carry a First-aid 
kit with them, and I am sure there 
are no exceptions to this rule. Here 
are some suggestions, however, regard¬ 
ing the contents: A waterproof box 
with rounded edges is ideal for carry¬ 
ing in packs, and can easily be taped 
to any canoe. Water purifier, insect 
repellent (such as D-12) and sunburn 
salve are also essential. Salt tablets, 
antiseptic, tape, gauze, and cotton 
should also be included, and most 
campers need a small darning needle 
with which to remove splinters. One 
important item which is often neglect¬ 
ed is the first-aid manual, a tiny book 
which ought never to be omitted. Also, 
include a pair of scissors. 

There is one piece of equipment 
which I doubt many camps provide 
for canoe trips. This is mosquito net- 
continued on page 27 


15 


The field of organized camping is 
growing faster than the statisticians 
can record. The Ontario Department 
of Education alone records nearly 
five hundred non-profit camps in 
their files. The Canadian Camping 
Association membership of about three 
hundred camps represents only a frac¬ 
tion of all the existing camps in Cana¬ 
da. Many new camps are founded 
each year by churches, service clubs, 
social agencies or individuals. As a 
camp owner-director, who has just 
gone through the process of finding, 
purchasing and developing a new 
camp site, I would like to pass on a 
few hints that might help others to 
avoid the many pitfalls that lie along 
the way. Any one mistake could not 
only be costly, it could be disastrous. 


that will serve to guide the “camp 
site selection” committee in their 
search. Why is this camp being estab¬ 
lished? Whom will it serve? (Age 
groups, numbers, type of campers) A 
site serving physically handicapped 
children would naturally need special 
consideration. From what cities will 
the campers be drawn? Will the camp 
site ever be enlarged? How much 
money can you afford to pay for a 
site? 

A virgin site allows one the freedom 
to build everything new and to one’s 
own specifications. However, at today’s 
building prices, the cost can be stag¬ 
gering if not prohibitive. Finding a 
partially cleared and developed site 
(e.g.) a farm, a lodge or a small camp 


SELECTING A CAMP SITE?. 


Unfortunately, mistakes don’t become 
evident until the developing and 
operating stages—when it is too late 
to reverse your course and it is costly 
to remedy. 

First, establish a camp committee 
with broad representation. Some mem¬ 
bers should have a strong camping 
background, others will have financial, 
legal, engineering, building, business, 
educational and parental backgrounds 
to suggest but a few possibilities. Build 
a committee that will bring rich and 
varied experience to your meetings. A 
camp with a strong committee has a 
solid foundation. 

The camp committee should estab¬ 
lish written objectives for the camp 


is initially cheaper but is often a 
compromise of what is desired. 

Appoint a small, temporary sub¬ 
committee to select the camp site. 
This committee should include the 
camp director, someone else with a 
strong camping background plus such 
people as an architect, a builder, a 
financial person, plus a lawyer. This 
is a technical committee. 

At the outset the sub-committee 
should be warned that finding the 
right site is difficult, in fact, it can be 
downright discouraging. I know 
people who have been looking for 
eight or ten years for the right site— 
without success. 

Knowing the principal city or cities 
from which your campers will be 


16 


Canadian Camping 






drawn, you should determine how 
many miles you are willing to travel 
to reach camp. Remember that what 
seems like wilderness or great distance 
today will probably be a burgeoning 
holiday center reached by direct, fast 
roads within a few years. All of us 
can think of such examples within 
our own memories. Therefore, do not 
be timid about reaching out into less 
developed areas; prices will be in 
direct relationship to the density of 
population. 

Check the policy governing crown 
lands in your province. In some prov¬ 
inces the number of acres available to 
any one camp are far too small for 
camping purposes. If available in large 
enough tracts, this land will be cheap- 


After you look at from ten to 
twenty sites, they will become fuzzy 
in your memory. In order to be able 
to compare sites, I set up a form that 
gave me essential information on each 
site visited. In this way the merits of 
each site can be weighted against the 
others and the number narrowed 
down to a few “good” prospects. 
These should then be revisited. It is 
surprising how different a site will 
look when seen for the second time. 
Never buy until you have seen a site 
two, or even three, times over a 
period of weeks. 

Before making a final decision, it 
would be wise to bring in some out¬ 
side, unbiased consultant, probably 
someone from the provincial camping 


.JUMP IN SLOWLY 

Barry G. Lowes, Director, Camp Timberlane. 


est. However, it will also be the least 
accessible and least developed. 

Real estate men in the outlying 
areas can often save you months and 
thousands of miles of fruitless wander¬ 
ings over bumpy back roads. Outline 
your requirements and circulate these 
to real estate agents. When possible 
sites have been submitted to you, map 
out a weekend itinerary that will en¬ 
able the committee to visit a number 
of prospective sites during one trip 
north. Some sites will rule themselves 
out at first sight but others will be 
worthy of consideration. Resign your¬ 
self to the fact that you will not find 
the “IDEAL” site. You will have to 
compromise on some things.

association, with considerable experi¬ 
ence. Experienced, objective eyes can 
often see things that an emotionally 
involved committee will overlook. 

Points of Consideration For 

The Selection Committee: 
Water Supply: 

If the water supply and drainage 
are poor—don’t waste time looking 
any further. What is the source? Sub¬ 
mit a sample for testing before final 
purchasing. Is the volume great en¬ 
ough all summer for all uses (kitchen, 
laundry, toilets, fire fighting, etc.). Be¬ 
ware of wells, they have a habit of 
running dry in August. Does any 
habitation or industry pose a threat 
to the water’s purity? 

turn to next page 
17 





Drainage: 

Getting water is usually easy. It is 
getting rid of it that poses the biggest 
problem in camp maintenance. What 
kind of soil is it? (Sand, loam, clay, 
rock, etc.) Is it low lying or swampy? 
Will sewage seep into your lake or 
settle in low lying areas? How would 
you dispose of wastes on this site? 

General Topography: 

How large is the site? (One acre 
per camper is recommended) Is the 
site on high ground or low land, hilly 
or flat? Is there some cleared land 
suitable for buildings and playfields? 
Arc there a generous number of 
wooded acres? Does it lend itself to 
natural divisions for decentralized 
camping? How much shore line is 
there? What is it like? (Steep, slop¬ 
ing, rocky, sandy, etc.) Is the site 
beautiful? 

Buildings: 

Are the existing buildings suitable 
for camp use? What would their re¬ 
placement value be? How much will 
it cost to move or convert them for 
camp use? 

Swimming Area: 

What is the nature of the bottom? 
(Sandy, muddy, rocky). Is it gently 
sloping or does it drop off suddenly? 
(Extremely dangerous). Are there 
weeds, leeches? Is the water clear or 
murky? What is the source of the 
lake water? Who controls the level 
of the water? (This is serious since 
some lakes drop eight feet over the 
summer months). How big is it? Is 
there a beach? Which direction would 
the swimming area face? Which way 
does the prevailing wind blow? Is it 
a rough lake? Is it safe for boating? 
What is the average summer tempera¬ 


ture of the water? How deep is the 
lake? How deep is the swimming 
area? Are there any underwater 
hazards? Can the area be developed 
into a safe, attractive waterfront area? 

Neighbours: 

Who else resides on the lake? Who 
owns the rest of the property? Will 
you have privacy? Can you get an 
option to purchase more land as pro¬ 
tection against the ever increasing en¬ 
croachment of cottages, speed boats, 
skiers and too many people? 

BUY AS MUCH LAND AS POSSI¬ 
BLE. It will never be cheaper. Or 
else you may wake up one morning 
to find a city-type cottage subdivision 
on your doorstep. Is there any fur¬ 
ther community or industrial develop¬ 
ment possible or planned for the area, 
which would affect the camp? It may 
be wilderness today but within a- few 
years a public road serving cottagers 
on the lake could run right through 
the middle of your camp. 

Tripping: 

Explore maps of the area. Are there 
chains of lakes suitable for canoe 
tripping? Who owns the lakes? Are 
camp sites available? Where will 
cook-outs and overnights go to camp? 
Is there fishing in the lake? Is there 
any poison ivy or oak? Poisonous 
snakes? 

T ransportation: 

How far is the nearest town? How 
far is the nearest paved highway? 
How long is the camp road? What 
condition is it in? Who maintains it? 
Is the road kept open year round? 
How will campers be transported to 
camp? Where is the closest railway 
depot? 

Services: 

Is electric power available? Tele¬ 
phone? How far is the closest hospital? 


18 


Canadian Camping 



Doctor? Post Office? Church? Forest 
Ranger Station? Fire Department? 
Closest dairy? Bread supply? Gro¬ 
ceries, meats and other foods? Garb¬ 
age dump? Laundry? Lumber com¬ 
pany? Plumbers? Electricians? Motel 
or lodges for visiting parents? Is local 
labour available? 

Legal: 

Do not consider purchasing any pro¬ 
perty without competent legal advice. 
Many properties have never been sur¬ 
veyed. Boundaries are often vaguely 
defined. Liens on properties are com¬ 
mon. Make sure the owner has clear 
title to the property. Some properties 
have unusual conditions attached to 
their deeds giving special rights to in¬ 
dividuals or development companies. 
Be certain that you have the mineral 
and timber rights to your property. 

This list is not exhaustive. However, 
if you have considered all of these 
points before purchasing a camp site, 
you will be buying with your eyes 
open, and your problems should be 
small ones once you start to build and 
develop. 

Before making a final decision, walk 
over and over your property. Try to 
project your imagination ahead five to 
ten years. How could this site look 
ultimately? Mentally lay out the camp. 
This will soon show up any defects. 
Don’t get carried away with enthusi¬ 
asm at this stage; be realistic. 

Once you have purchased the pro¬ 
perty, draw up a Master Plan that 
puts the camp on paper. Plot every 
area and building as it will appear 
ultimately. Plan years ahead, assigning 
priorities and anticipated costs. Every 
building, every clearing, every dollar 
spent will be a piece of the larger pic¬ 
ture fitting into place. 


It is an exciting, challenging ex¬ 
perience. Good luck. 

A copy of a suggested form to 
guide committees in selecting a site 
may be had free by writing to the 
Ontario Camping Association.

DOS' AND DON'TS 


DON’T handle foods while you have an open sore or boil on your hands, 
forearms, or face. 

DON’T handle food if you have a sore throat or sinusitis, or have recently 
recovered from typhoid or diarrhea. 

DON’T use cooking spoons or forks to taste food while cooking or serving. 

DON’T lick your fingers while you are working with food. 

DON’T use dried eggs except for baking. They may contain salmonella bacteria 
which can cause illness unless the product in which they are used is thoroughly 
cooked. 

DON’T serve cream puddings, cream pies, or cream puffs unless you can refri¬ 
gerate them as soon as they are prepared. Keep them in the refrigerator until 
they are served. 

DON’T use canned food if the ends of the can are bulged, if the can leaks or 
if liquid gushes out when the can is opened. The food is spoiled and should be 
thrown out. Discard any canned food that is mushy, slimy, moldy, or has a 
soft appearance or an unpleasant odor. 

DON’T taste any canned food that is suspected of spoilage. It may cause food 
poisoning, and should be thrown out immediately. 

DO use water from a safe municipal supply or from another source known to 
be of good sanitary quality. 

DO wash your hands often with soap and warm water, especially after you use 
the toilet. Keep your hands away from your mouth and nose. 

DO regard your hands as contaminated. Keep them out of food as much as 
you can, and away from dish surfaces that come in contact with the campers’ 
lips. Learn to pick up glasses at the base, and cups and silver by the handles. 


20 


Canadian Camping 






FOR FOOD HANDLERS 

Ruth Carruthers, Dietitian, 

Camps Bolton and Illahee, 
Neighbourhood Workers Association, 
Toronto. 


DO wear clean, washable clothes and a cap or hair net. 

DO use only pasteurized milk and cream, and ice cream, butter, and cheese 
made from pasteurized milk or cream. 

DO buy meats that bear the federal inspection stamp, or are from at locally 
inspected source. 

DO cook pork till a meat thermometer registers an internal temperature of 185 
degrees F. 

DO serve oysters and. clams only from approved sources. You can determine 
whether the source is approved by checking the labels against a list of approved 
shippers and dealers obtainable from state or city health officers. 

DO boil vigorously for 15 minutes such home-canned, nonacid foods as peas 
and string beans. 

DO keep your kitchen free from flies, roaches, rats, and mice. 

DO label poisons; store them apart from your food. Too often, white, powdered 
insecticides have been mistaken for sugar or flour. 

DO keep fresh foods and cooked foods that must be held for several hours in 
the refrigerator at a temperature between 35 degrees and 42 degrees F. Meats, 
particularly tenderized ham, will spoil if they are held at room temperature for 
long periods after cooking. Ham and held-over chicken and turkey are frequent¬ 
ly the cause of bacterial food poisoning. 

DO practice good housekeeping. Wash tabletops and other work surfaces every 
time you use them. Defrost and clean refrigerators at a regular time each 
week. Keep your storeroom clean and orderly. Wash meat grinders and meat 
sheers thoroughly, immediately after you use them. If these pieces of equipment 
are not washed as soon as they are used, germs will multiply in the meat parti¬ 
cles that remain in them, and may cause illness.

LET’S GO CAMPING 

By Dorothy H. Davis 


Frankly, I do not know of any rea¬ 
son why parents of an average child 
or children would not want to send 
their children to a well run summer 
camp. Camping can provide an ex¬ 
perience and set of values for child¬ 
ren, that will serve them all their 
lives. 

A family camp offers chidren an 
abundance of activities and a great 
fund of knowledge. They learn to 
amuse themselves by collecting items 
for a museum, building a tree-house 
or a raft, or watching a turtle laying 
eggs. They see and respect the awe of 
a thunderstorm, the beauty of a sun¬ 
rise and sunset. The child should have 
certain responsibilities to fulfill, but 
should also have time to relax and 
think, and wonder. Mental health is 
as important as physical health, and 
I feel that both are benefited by camp¬ 
ing. 

My husband and I have four child¬ 
ren—two girls twenty and eighteen, 
and two boys twelve and ten. Both 
girls and the eldest boy have attended 
non-profit summer camps with results 
that are very satisfactory from both 
their point of view and ours. 

The girls started ^ their organized 
camping as members of one of the 


finest youth organizations in the 
world — the Girl Guides. They ex¬ 
perienced living under what I con¬ 
sider to be the best form of camping 
—living under canvas. They slept on 
straw palliasses, cooked out of doors, 
and lived in close proximity to other 
girls of a similar age group, but with 
varying backgrounds, interests and 
other personal attributes. They lived 
close to nature and explored it’s won¬ 
ders. They experienced healthy physi¬ 
cal and mental exercises, and most 
important, they experienced personal 
relationship with other girl counsellors 
and senior staff, that enabled them to 
find themselves and orient themselves 
to authority, self-reliance, initiative, 
responsibility, and tolerance. They 
learned the beauty and reverence of 
outdoor worship. 

They have camped elsewhere, and 
have been most fortunate in their 
camp directors, counsellors, and camp 
facilities. These latter are what make 
good or bad impressions of camping, 
and in regard to these matters, the 
parents must make adequate investi¬ 
gation before sending a child to a 
camp. 

Our boys are younger and the eld¬ 
est only has attended a camp other

NEVER AGAIN ! 

By Margaret O. Edwards 


We sent our boy to camp—ONCE! 
Of course, the things that happened 
to him, would not necessarily happen 
to anyone else. And as we look back 
at this disastrous experience, we rea¬ 
lize that there were precautions we 
should have taken. 

Since neither my husband nor my¬ 
self had ever been to camp, we had a 
very casual approach to the whole 
thing. I had picked up a descriptive 
folder at a Home and School meet¬ 
ing. It stressed, amongst other things, 
the joys of learning to swim at an 
early age and this convinced us. We 
should have known that a child eight 
years old is much too young for a 
camp. 

Without meeting the Director, with¬ 
out enquiring about counsellors, with¬ 
out seeing the campsite, without even 
contacting parents who might have 
sent a child to this particular camp, 
we forwarded our fee and in due 
course received the list of necessary 
equipment. 

Little realizing that our son would 
have to locate and handle his baggage 
single handed, we packed bag upon 
bag with the suggested gear. It took 
three of us to get it to the bus and 
there we were disconcerted to note 
that everybody’s clothing seemed to 


be encased in airforce blue bags. We 
had a premonition that his baggage 
would be hard to locate—which it 
was! 

That first week of his holiday, we 
imagined him having a glorious time, 
in the great outdoors and becoming a 
swimmer, in due course. Visiting day 
was eagerly awaited and off we drove 
to see things for ourselves, at last. 

As we turned into the grounds, we 
suddenly hesitated. As far as the eye 
could see, were great stretches of poi¬ 
son ivy. Rolling up socks, pulling 
down longs, we gingerly stepped out 
and mingled with the other fearful 
visitors. 

We met dozens of campers. Most 
of them had running eyes and running 
sores on their arms and legs. Yes, that’s 
right, POISON IVY! But no one 
knew our boy well enough to have 
any idea of his whereabouts. At last 
we encountered a lad who did. “Oh 
yes, Bun Edwards. Nice little boy. 
He’s in the hospital!” 

The hospital was a neat, pleasant 
enough building and it was filled to 
capacity (you guessed it) with poison 
ivy cases. Our boy had merely turned 
his ankle and was being bandaged.

BOYS’ BOOK OF 
OUTBOARD BOATING 

By Tom Parsons 

This rather awkward title detracts 
not at all from the excellence of this 
small book. With outboards becoming 
so increasingly popular on all Cana¬ 
dian waters, a book setting out so suc¬ 
cinctly for the young the proper choos¬ 
ing, handling and care of an outboard 
motor is very welcome. There are ex¬ 
cellent chapters on Rules of the Road, 
signals, etc., as well as a short and 
needful reminder that the “man at 
the tiller” is the most important thing 
about the boat. Whether it should 
have a place in a Camp Library is 
debatable as few camps allow their 
campers to choose, service or indeed 
run their boats. However as a begin¬ 
ner’s book of outboard motor care it 
is well worth having for reference. 

Brett-Macmillan Publishing Co., 
Galt, Ontario. $2.50. 


A GUIDE FOR TRAINERS OF 
GIRL SCOUT LEADERS 

As its name suggests, this book is 



by Joyce Bertram 


more concerned with methods used by 
the Girl Scout movement in the U.S. 
than with camping. There are how¬ 
ever. suggestions which could be 
adapted for counsellor training pro¬ 
grams in Canadian Camps. 

Girl Scouts of the United States of 
America. $2.00. 


WORKING WITH THE 
HANDICAPPED 

This also has been written for the 
Girl Scout movement, but bring to 
our attention some excellent sugges¬ 
tions in the treatment of handicapped 
children through recreation. While 
it does not deal specifically with the 
camping program per se it does em¬ 
phasize once again how important it 
is for the child who is not “normal”. 
The first two or three chapters would 
be particularly helpful for anyone who 
is contemplating working, either at 
camp or in the city, with the handi¬ 
capped child. 

Girl Scouts of the United States of 
America, 830 Third Avc., New York, 
22, N.Y. 75 cents.

THE ANGLERS’ BOOK OF 
CANADIAN FISHES 

By F. H. Wooding 

According to Gregory Clark in his 
foreword to this book, fifty years ago 
a fisherman had to be “rich, idle and/ 
or daft” before he could hope to be¬ 
come a successful angler. But now that 
easy means of transportation bring so 
many rivers and lakes within com¬ 
muting distance, it is the exceptional 
family who does not boast a rabid 
fisherman who is neither rich, idle 
nor daft. This fisherman will fall 
upon Mr. Wooding’s book with loud 
cries of delight. Many books set out 
in detail how and where to land cer¬ 
tain fish, but this one attempts to 
give information about all fish indi¬ 
genous to Canadian waters. Each sec¬ 
tion gives a detailed description of the 
particular fish and then goes on to 
describe how and where to catch it. 
Should keep the fisherman of the 
family happily employed all winter. 

Collins Publishing Co., Toronto. 
$6.95. 

X1NGU 

By Violette and John Viertel 

This little book is an enchanting 
tale of a boy on the shores of the 
Amazon River in South America. His 
friends are the various animals which 
frequent that locale and some of them 
are quite charming—some of them are 
NOT so quite! But then Xingu is 
given a bow and arrow for his birth¬ 
day and playfully shoots his dearest 
friend the vicuna. Chasing the vicuna 
through the jungle, little Xingu 
realizes what a lonely and scarey 
place it is with none of his familiar 
friends about. But he is forgiven by 
his wounded friend and all the other 
animals, and promises to plant seeds 
and roots and live from the land 
rather than to go hunting any more. 
Illustrations are by Karla Kuskin. 


Brett-Macmillan Publishing Co., 
Galt, Ont. $2.75. 

CAMPSITE DEVELOPMENT 

By Julian Salomon 

This is an entirely new and en¬ 
larged edition of the book first pub¬ 
lished ten years ago. In that interven¬ 
ing space of time many changes have 
taken place in building trends, and 
this book shows very clearly that there 
is no quarrel between the rustic type 
of construction favoured by many 
camps, and the use of new materials. 
Although intended originally for all 
those concerned with planning and 
building Girl Scout camping facilities, 
it will doubtless prove to be an ex¬ 
cellent reference book for any inter¬ 
ested in camp site development, parti¬ 
cularly if they are lucky enough to be 
starting from scratch. This book is 
lavishly illustrated with all types of 
buildings from tent platforms to split 
level lodges. It is a most valuable book 
for all directors and camp planning 
boards. 

Girl Scouts of the U.S.A., 830 Third 
Ave, New York 22, N.Y. $5. 

GIRL SCOUTS’ NATURE QUIZ 
BOOKLET A CHALLENGE 
TO ALL AGES 

Is the upper lip of a rabbit split? 
Do all birds have hollow bones? Any¬ 
one versed in the questions and an¬ 
swers in True and False, an up-to- 
date pocket quiz booklet published by 
the Girl Scouts of the U.S.A., will 
know these questions immediately. 

Whimsically illustrated in pen and 
ink, True and False, explodes the 
myths and superstitions held by many 
adults about the Animal, Vegetable 
and Mineral worlds. 

To prove the point, merely ask the 
self-appointed “expert” if a giraffe 
can bellow like an elephant. Odds are,

continued from page 10 

4. Retire early and rise early. The 
evening meal should be completed well 
before dark. 

5. Leave the campsite better than you 
found it. Make sure you do not leave 
any of your belongings behind. These 
are signs of a good camper. 


Safety: 

1. SWIMMING—There must be rules 
on a trip as well as in camp. Check 
the area for submerged rocks or logs. 
Swim parallel to the shore, not out 
from it. Swimming takes place only 
when and where the trip leader says. 
Use the Buddy System with one 
counsellor acting as lifeguard. 

2. CANOEING — When travelling, 
canoes should stay together. At the 
campsite the leader should determine 
the “canoeing area” and keep one 
canoe on shore for rescue purposes. 

3. CHOPPING — Find out who can 
handle an axe before leaving camp. 
Then only permit those who have 
some skill to chop while on a trip, 
and then under supervision. A bad 
cut can spoil the trip for everyone. 

4. FIRST AID—Make sure you know 
first aid and artificial respiration. Al¬ 
ways know the fastest way home. 
Have an emergency plan. 

5. KNOW— 

(a) How to avoid getting lost. 

(b) What to do if you are lost. 


(c) How to prevent the canoe 
from tipping. 

(d) What to do if the canoe does 
tip. 

(e) How to make a safe fire and 
put it out. 

(f) What to do to keep dry in 
wet weather. 


General: 

1. Enjoy the trip. Learn as much as 
you can about the out-of-doors, the 
weather signs, the best way to do 
things. The more your knowledge in¬ 
creases about tripping, the more you 
will enjoy it. 

2. Encoyrage the taking of notes and 
writing trip reports. Those who do 
will get more out of the trip. Have 
every member of the party follow the 
map as you go along, so that all will 
know where they are going. 

3. Instruct campers as you go along. 
Point out interesting things. Tell 
them the names of the various trees, 
and wild flowers. Talk and sing to¬ 
gether. 

4. Endeavour not to get wet, above all, 
do not stay wet. It is a miserable feel¬ 
ing and nothing will dampen your 
enthusiasm for trips as much. Learn 
how to camp in wet weather. 

5. Let the campers do the work. Guide 
them and help them, but let them do 
as much as their age and ability per¬ 
mit. The more they do, the more they 
will learn, and the more they will en¬ 
joy the trip.

child and offer some help.

well-adjusted adults. Through troubl¬ 
ed waters as well as calm, we believe 
their camping experiences have given 
them intangible assets upon which 
they can always rely.

Crafts Materials 

Donated by Mother Nature 

Very few camps have an unlimited 
budget for crafts materials, but at 
every camp site nearly all, and at 
least some, of the following weeds 
and pods grow along the roadside or 
at the water’s edge. There they are, 
free for the gathering, ready to be 
enthusiastically mixed with the im- 
amgination and initiative of your 
crafts counsellor: 

CORN HUSKS, CAT TAILS, 
GRASSES can be gathered when full 
grown, dried and hung for drying. 
Moisten them for use, experiment with 
dyes if you wish colour, and use them 
for weaving or braiding. 

CAT TAIL OR MILKWEED POD 
FLUFF can be used for stuffing toys. 
NUTS AND ACORNS can be cut 
with a saw (carefully) and used for 
earrings, neckerchief holders, brooches, 
bracelets, place cards and other novel¬ 
ties as far as the imagination can 
conceive. 

WILLOW for whistles. 

CLAY may be fired and glazed. Keep 
your eyes open. It’s surprising how 
often small clay deposits occur in 
sandy areas.

Toronto, Canada, December 1959 


29 





NATURE 

TOOLS 

Bettye Breeser 

Reprinted from Recreation Magazine. 


Mrs. Breeser is a member of the Pennsyl¬ 
vania section of the American Camping 
Association, and was chairman of the 
Downingtown Area In-Camp Nature Insti¬ 
tute, 1956, a Comstock Society executive 
board member, and past president of the 
Professional Writers Club of Philadelphia. 
She has had twenty years camping experi¬ 
ence, with eight years as a camp director. 


Nature is one of the easiest sub¬ 
jects to present to campers, for it is 
all around them. However, directors 
are constantly faced with the prob¬ 
lem of getting a good nature counsel¬ 
lor who can inspire and interest young¬ 
sters. Rather than having one special¬ 
ist in the field, it is better that all 
counsellors, from the water-front in¬ 
structor to the camp nurse, be aware 
of the never-ending challenge of on- 
the-spot nature. 

One man, hired by a camp, pre¬ 
sented an excellent unscheduled na¬ 
ture session to some happy campers 
when he discovered a small rabbit 
family while mowing a field. The child¬ 
ren’s delight in making their own 
nest for imaginary play highlighted 
worthwhile creative activities as well 
as wildlife conservation. 

Campers who dub a maple the 
“nose tree” are being exposed to good 
nature study, for their fun in wearing 
a split seed flyer on their nose is a 
fine firsthand experience in observa¬ 
tion, and they will long remember the 
maple in this connection. Perhaps the 


name “crying tree” is a little far¬ 
fetched, but lucky are the youngsters 
with the counsellor who points out the 
beechnut’s teardrop shape. Long ago 
joys of youth included such things as 
shooting a narrow-leaf plantain top 
and being able to blow a blade of 
grass. Children today, in spite of a 
life geared to television, radio and 
movies, arc still happy to blow a dan¬ 
delion’s white top and test their chins 
with a buttercup to see if they like 
butter. 

Conservation must start early with 
youth, for too many years have al¬ 
ready passed with people destroying 
rather than enjoying nature. Diking a 
camp stream to make pools for small 
fish during dry spells has a two-way 
advantage: the preservation of flippers 
and an excellent water program for 
the campers. It’s easy for children to 
dam a stream, and mud oozing up 
between the toes is an elixir unrivalled. 
Critter life in any stream is unpre¬ 
dictable and exciting, and there’s an 
inexplicable thrill in catching the first 
frog, turtle, salamander or crawfish. 

The common jewelweed or touch- 
me-not crowds many of our camp 
streams, but how many campers are 
ever told that the plant usually has 
bright red “toes” (roots), and that the 
leaves when submerged turn silver? 
How about the reed worms in those 
browning grass stalks when they want 



30 


Canadian Camping 


to fish? Digging worms isn’t always 
easy, but there’s bait under rocks and 
in the reeds for those who explore. 

The young whittler who craves to 
carve his name on the nearest tree 
can be encouraged to do a bit of con¬ 
servation with his knife. Replanting 
eroded stream banks with freshly cut 
willow shoots is an excellent nature 
program. 

Encouraging children to see at all 
three levels is wise, for there’s just as 
much to enjoy in the vastness of the 
sky as on the ant level. To lie down 
in a field is to open up a new world 
to a camper. These minutes of viewing 
will offer a world of fantasy as the 
child sees cloud witches, animals, 
castles and imaginary characters float¬ 
ing above. There’s still joy in pulling 
off the petals of the daisy to see if 
“he loves me, he loves me not,” and 
a daisy wreath still tops the list of 
childhood crafts. 

By a stretch of the imagination, a 
grove of trees can well become a 
camp’s “castle.” Through the shaded 
paths boys and girls can create a 
simple yet worthwhile enchanted trail. 
The counsellor who stimulates this 
project by offering some cleverly post¬ 
ed signs is well on his way to a good 
nature project. “Step through this 
tree and make a wish!” can spark the 
first lap of such a trail, followed by a 
note on a stump that reads, “The 
magic throne—sit on it and your wish 
will come true!” 

“This is the birds’ opera house — 
listen!” will encourage silence near a 
thicket, with a notice further on sug¬ 
gesting that “The mitten tree (sassa¬ 
fras) grows close by—can you find any 
left-handed ones?” An arched grove of 
locust trees might suggest the “tun¬ 
nel of the giants,” and a tangle of 
honey-suckle the “home of the wicked 


witch!” All this is nature interwoven 
with creative play and offers any 
camp leader unending possibilities. 

Assorted burrs that grow along 
wooded trails can be used for clever 
table decorations. With the addition of 
two small green leaves they assume 
shapes of insects to top ferns or flow¬ 
ers in a bouquet. The common May 
apple, arranged with twigs, can be¬ 
come a coy duck, peacock, or camp 
“happy bird.” 

Plays and stories dealing with na¬ 
ture are vital in a camp setting. 
Young actors are naturals when they 
are performing on a soft, wooded 
stage, and lessons learned are long 
remembered. The child who makes a 
helmet of red oak leaves will know 
the spine tips of the tree. He will long 
remember the music of the stream as 
he said his brief part in a play with 
the scent of the freshly cut spicebush 
as the backdrop. 

Creative writing is a valuable tool 
for nature. Stories written about a 
tree, flower, shrub, or animal found 
in camp can well evolve into panto¬ 
mime dramatics. Children are not al¬ 
ways deft with the mechanics of writ¬ 
ing, but a wise counsellor jots down 
their thinking, and catches their vivid 
imagination as stories are told. 

The reflection of blue sky on a Vir¬ 
ginia creeper leaf may suggest the 
sky’s looking glass to some campers, 
while a story of the magic umbrellas 
may come from knowing the May 
apple. Galls are intriguing, and some 
child may chance to write a story on 
how the elves place tiny “fried eggs” 
on maple leaves. 

Counting age rings on a tree could 
well suggest a story on the imaginary 
history of the tree. Did Indians ever 
camp beneath its shade, and what 
years suffered drought? The widest 


Toronto, Canada, December 1959 


31 



rings usually appear on the north 
side, or dampest portion of the tree, 
which brings into focus the subject of 
finding direction without a compass. 

All grasses arc not the same. Why 
not make a booklet of the collection in 
camp? The graceful specimens, 
mounted on black construction paper 
and covered with a clear plastic film 
arc longlasting and educational. Danc¬ 
ing dolls from long-needled pines will 
keep many a young miss happy for 
hours. Pretty stones, mounted in plas¬ 
ter of Paris are unique paperweights 
to be taken home as a souvenir. 

Campfires are also nature, for the 
direction of the smoke can well fore¬ 
cast the expected weather. By just 
listening, too, campers can tell if rain 
is due by the distant whistles. Their 
sense of smell is keen and the wise 
counsellor is ever on the alert to recog¬ 
nize the ozone after a rain, the fresh¬ 
ness ol a woods in the morning and 
the fragrance of new mown hay. 

The cracking of twigs and dry 
leaves on a southern slope should be 
pointed out to campers to compare 
with the quiet spongy footing they ex¬ 
perience on a northern hillside. Coun¬ 
try children for decades have found 
pleasure in chewing sourgrass (wood 
sorrel), mint, spiccbush, sassafras and 
the like, and there’s still a big thrill 
in catching the large drop of nectar 
from the top of a honeysuckle blossom. 


All campers should know the 
slippery inner bark of a willow twig, 
for whistle making was a craft of our 
forefathers. Dandelion stems make ex¬ 
cellent curls when split and dropped 
in water. Violets and many other wild 
flowers explode their pods when ripe. 
Are these the “sharpshooters” of the 
woods? Nature materials are found in 
almost all camp settings, even in city 
parks. The “throw-aways” ol nature, 
such as pods, seeds, shedding bark 
and leaves, are naturecraft materials 
to the counsellor with imagination. 

Campers should have time to watch 
the bees in a hollyhock and see the 
backward flight of a humming bird as 
he leaves a blossom. They should catch 
fireflies and watch ants at work in 
their mounds. The feel ol moist grass 
at sunup should be theirs and their 
eyes should marvel at the panorama of 
color at sunset. 

They should see their own reflec¬ 
tion in a stream and the mirrored 
leaves overhead. The softness of moss 
should not be strange to young feet 
nor the powdery dust of a camp lane. 
Their hands should be stained with 
the juice of wild strawberries, and 
they should know the milky fluid that 
seeps from the stem of the milkweed. 
This is nature the easy way. Intensi¬ 
fied study and identification will come 
in later years after appreciation and 
love of the out-of-doors has been well 
rooted in camp.

This was the second time. The first 
occurred on his first day at the Camp. 
Exit dreams of learning to swim, since 
he had not been allowed in the water 
with his swollen foot. Carelessness, we 
agreed, until he hobbled out with us 
and took us on a tour of the campsite. 

More mountainous terrain, we never 
hope to see. He was lucky he hadn't 
sprained his back. The tents were 
pitched on a hill and the excitement 
of the evening was to see if the tent 
would fall down in the night. 

We now discovered that most of his 
bedding could not be located. He and 
another little boy had pooled the 
couple of blankets they could find and 
were sleeping on the floorboards, in a 
huddle, reminiscent of a rat’s nest. 
Luxuries, such as a hat, pen, flash¬ 
light were nowhere to be found. 

The swimming area also proved dis¬ 
appointing. A pile of sand at one end 
would have improved the beach, but 
no one had had the strength to 
spread it. The water looked dirty, and 
foreign objects floated about on it. We 
decided that a sprained ankle could 
be a blessing. 

There was a new, very pleasant din¬ 
ing hall, where crafts were taught on 
rainy days. Aside from this, we found 
very little to recommend this garden 
spot of holiday retreats. 

Quite naturally, we felt we’d like to 
meet the Director or counsellor. No¬ 
where could they be located. In fact, 
aside from the Camp nurse, there 
didn’t seem to be anyone over twelve 
in attendance. 

Which brought up the question, 
“Should we leave the boy?” 

Now here we found ourselves facing 
a rather subtle form of mental black¬ 
mail. If a child left a camp before the 
allotted time, there was something 
wrong with him. Never with the 
camp, just with him!

A GUIDE POST TO 
SAFE WATER SKIING 

Harold M. Gore 


Water skiing is believed to have 
had its origin twenty-five years ago 
among French ski troops who develop¬ 
ed this new type of recreation by turn¬ 
ing their snow ski abilities to the 
water. Now more and more snow ski¬ 
ers are following the same process of 
evolution. At first the sport was re¬ 
served for those who owned a speed¬ 
boat with a powerful inboard motor. 
In recent years the low-cost outboard 
motor has all but wiped out financial 
barriers and brought water skiing 
within easy reach of the average in¬ 
come. Since so many youngsters are 
turning to the thrills of skimming 
across the water on a pair of wooden 
boards, we might plan to include this 
new sport in the aquatic program. 

Water skiing is not difficult and 
does not require exceptional athletic 
ability. Almost anyone can learn to do 
it well enough to have fun. The funda¬ 
mentals can be learned in a matter of 
hours. In many camps, waterfront 
leaders can readily set up a safe water 
skiing program if the methods are 
carefully explained to them. Here are 
the basic standards for this activity. 

Two Types of Training Needed 

Training a boy to ski is only half 
the training problem. Water skiing is 
tied in with and dependent upon out- 


Harold M. Gore is a member of the Na¬ 
tional Committee on Health and Safety, 
Boy Scouts of America, and director of 
Camp Najerog, Wilmington, Vermont. His 
article is reprinted from the bulletin. 
“Health and Safety,” and used by per¬ 
mission of the Boy Scouts of America. 


board boating, and a program of out¬ 
board boatsmanship must be offered 
in addition to training in skiing. This 
should include practice in safe boat 
handling, training in rules of the 
water road, and practice of courtesy 
afloat. 

Water skiing should conform to all 
regular waterfront requirements. 
Every skier should be a strong swim¬ 
mer and should be at home in, on, 
and under the water. 


Boats and Motors 

Two very important safety factors 
enter the picture at this point: (1) 
the selection of the proper boat and 
motor and (2) the teamwork develop¬ 
ed between a trained outboard motor- 
boat operator and the water skier. 

An ideal outboard hull is probably 
a fourteen-foot runabout with a wide 
transom, about fifty-four inches. 
Water skiers can skim along behind 


34 


Canadian Camping 



Reprinted from Recreation Magazine. 



such a boat powered with a seven- 
and-a-half- to ten-horsepower motor 
and work up a speed of from fifteen 
to twenty or more miles per hour. A 
wide stem is necessary. Towing a skier 
around a sharp turn can make steer¬ 
ing difficult and boat balance unstable 
if the stern is narrow. 

It is important to match boats and 
motors for best performance. If the 
motor is too small, it won’t pull the 
skier up out of the water. Even 
worse, if the motor is too large for 
the hull, the boat will be overpower¬ 
ed. That means danger and plenty of 
trouble afloat. Boats certified by the 
Outboard Boating Club of America 
carry a plate stating the recommend¬ 
ed maximum horsepower. 

Proper towrope attachments are im¬ 
portant. Lifting handles and motor 
clamps should not be used. Towropes 
should be attached to eyebolts installed 
on the transom. 

Many boats have capsized when 
towing a skier in a tight turn. There 
should be at least one life jacket or 
cushion for every person on board. 
Other essentials in the boat include 
oars or paddles, ample lines, whistle or 
horn, first-aid kit, a knife, fire extin¬ 
guisher, extra shear pins for motor, 
extra plugs, and a tool kit. 

A Good Boatman 

The water skier’s partner in good 
skiing teamwork is the boat driver. We 
go along with those folks who feel 
that the boat driver is ninety per cent 


of safe skiing! The water skier’s safety 
may depend on how well the boat is 
handled. 

There should always be two men in 
the boat: a driver to operate the boat 
and look ahead so that he can steer 
the boat and skier away from possible 
danger spots and an observer to 
watch the skier and give orders to the 
driver. 

The Skier’s Equipment 

The equipment for water skiing in¬ 
cludes skis, binding, and towrope. The 
outboard-style ski is recommended for 
beginners. These are usually about six 
feet long and seven inches wide. Bind¬ 
ings are usually made of a flexible ma¬ 
terial like gum rubber, so that they 
will give way in case of a fall, and pre¬ 
vent ankle injuries. Towropes are from 
sixty to seventy-five feet and have a 
towbar attached. 

The use of life vests or jackets is 
recommended for beginning skiers and 
is advisable for skiing on larger bod¬ 
ies of water or under unusual condi¬ 
tions such as cold water or rough 
weather. 

Getting Started 

Basic skiing can be learned in a very 
few lessons. It’s important to get start¬ 
ed correctly and not develop any bad 
habits in form. Points to remember: 
keep the knees bent, arms straight, 
and have the weight balanced directly 
over the feet, while in a half-crouch 
position. 

Start off with a little practice 
ashore. Dry-land exercise is used to 
teach proper position and balance and 
to get the “feel.” Then try actual 
starts in the water. 

turn to next page

When the skier is in the water and 
ready, the towboat starts at idling 
speed until the towrope is extended to 
its full length. The driver doesn’t “hit 
it” (apply full throttle) until the 
rope is taut, he can see the skier’s tips, 
and the skier has indicated that he is 
ready to go. It’s a real partnership 
between the skier and driver! 

When the skier is “up” on the 
water, power should be eased off as 
signaled by the skier — “thumbs up” 
meaning more speed, “thumbs down,” 
less speed. Wide-arc turns are pre¬ 
ferable. If a short turn is necessary, 
the driver should be sure the skier is 
not going to be on the inside of the 
turn. If the skier is outside the wake 
on the left (port) side, don’t turn 
left too sharply until he has returned 
to the wake. If he is on the inside he 
will sink because of lack of speed and, 
unless he lets go, will have the tow- 
rope pulled from his hands when the 
line finally straightens out. 

The boat driver must steer the 
skier away from all objects such as 
docks and sea walls and give other 
boats and obstacles a wide berth. He 
must avoid swimmers. 

When recovering a fallen skiier, cut 
speed immediately to determine if he 
is entangled in rope, then return 
quickly, coming up at idling speed, 
and make a half circle around him. 
This will bring the towline directly 
into his hands. Kill the motor when 
taking a skier into the boat, as he may 
slip and get hit by the prop. An idl¬ 
ing boat in neutral is not safe. 

In the take-off the skier puts on his 
skis in about two or three feet of 
water, grabs the towbar, and then 
raises the tips of his skis above the 
water as a signal to the driver to 
start the boat. When the boat starts 
to pull, the skier should allow it to 
pull him up slowly to a standing posi¬ 
tion. It’s important that the driver 
give the skier a fast but steady pull. 

turn to next page 


36 


Canadian Camping 



The skier does not pull up with his 
arms! Keep the arms straight at the 
take-off and let the boat do the pull¬ 
ing. 

Code of the Safe Water Skier 

• Learn to be a strong swimmer be¬ 
fore attempting to water ski. Sr. Red 
Cross, Royal Life Bronze or equival¬ 
ent. 

• Equipment should always be tested 
before skiing. 

• When starting, don’t yell “hit it” 
until your ski tips are up and the rope 
is taut. 

• Stay away from docks, sea walls, 
boats, and swimmers. Skiers seldom 
get hurt from hitting the water, but 
usually from striking solid objects. 

• Watch the water ahead. Skier 
must not depend on driver to keep 
him from dangerous objects. 

• Be thoughtful of the rights of 
swimmers, boatmen, and fishermen. 


• On falling: Recover skis, as they 
will keep you afloat. 

Raise hand quickly to signal boat 
driver. 

If in a congested area raise a ski so 
other boats can see you. 

Release the handle when falling 
backwards. 

Avoid falling forward into the rope. 

• Never wrap the towrope around 
the body. 

• Be very careful with the rope. 
Getting it tangled on take-off, or pull¬ 
ing up on it so that you have slack 
while skiing, could lead to trouble. 

• When landing, run parallel to 
shore, come in slowly, and release 
towbar a safe distance from shore. Do 
not land in swimming areas. 

• Don’t ski in shallow water. Avoid 
excessive speed. Ski progressively — 
the skier should never try stunts for 
which he does not have the basic skill.

How Well Do You Know Bats? 

Q. Where do bats spend the winter? 

A. Within a hollow tree, cave or pro¬ 
tected place. 

Q. Do bats move around during the 
winter? 

A. No! They sleep and awaken only 
when insects become active in the 
spring. 

Q. What bat is found all over On¬ 
tario including the far north? 

A. Little Brown Bat. 

Q. Do bats fly fast? 

A. Yes. Swifts and swallows are the 
only birds which fly as fast and 
can turn with such ease as bats. 

Q. How many young do bats have? 

A. One. 

Q. What does the mother bat do with 
her baby while seeking food? 

A. She often takes it with her and 
during the flight it clings to her 
neck. 

Q. What does a mother bat do with 
her baby if she does not want to 
take it on a flight in search of 
food? 

A. She hangs it on a twig by the 
little hooks attached to its small 
feet which project from the wings 
and are used by all bats when 
resting. 

Q. How do bats collect their food? 

A. Like swifts they fly with the 
mouth open. 


Q. What other method of capturing 
insects do bats have that no bird 
has? 

A. They double up their wings like 
an apron and scoop up insects and 
reach down to eat them. 

—Reprinted from The Young Naturalist, 
published by the Federation of Ontario 
Naturalists. 


How to Estimate Height of a Tree 

How tall is a certain tree? 

That is a question that frequently 
baffles observers looking at one of the 
giants of the forest. 

Actually there is a very simple method 
of estimating the correct figure. It is 
an old Indian one. 

It consists in walking away until you 
reach a point where you can bend over 
and see the tip of the tree from this 
position. You then walk from where 
you are to the base of the tree, counting 
off one foot for every step taken. The 
total footage will be the approximate 
height of the tree. 


Speaking of Skunks 

Skunks don’t have to be very old to 
be equipped with their peculiar defence 
mechanism. A Parry Sound resident 
was forced to stop to allow a mother 
•skunk and nine babies to cross the road 
and was so captivated by the little 
fellows that he got out of his car and 
captured two to take home. Lands and 
Forests Dept, officers reported: “Before 
arriving home he knew he had done the 
wrong thing. He was unable to rectify 
the situation because the little fellows 
were under the car seat and he couldn’t 
remove them without almost tearing the 
car apart. 

“Persons who admire small wild 
animals should remember that he who 
carries small skunks in his car rides 
alone.”

By Dr. Paul Little 




Dedication services in a rural 
church, for a new organ, included a 
concert by a famous organist from the 
city. The instrument was of the old 
type, propelled by means of hand 
bellows. 

The church was filled to capacity, 
and the organist was giving an ex¬ 
cellent recital. He was quite proud of 
himself as he walked backstage for a 
few moments during the intermission. 
There he encountered the old organ 
pumper, strolling around to ease his 
weary arms. 

“We’re giving a fine concert,” re¬ 
marked the old man. The proud 
organist pretended not to have heard 
it." 

“I say,” the old man ventured again, 
“we arc giving them a fine musicale.” 

The organist drew himself up 
haughtily. “We?” he exclaimed, “We 
—a fine concert? T beg your pardon— 
I am the performer!” And whirling 
on his heels he returned to the con¬ 
sole to give the rest of his programme. 

The first number in the second part 
was written for the full organ. The 
performer pulled out the necessary 


Toronto, Canada, December 1959 


stops, opened the Swell and Crescendo 
pedals to their limit, paused dramati¬ 
cally until the audience had become 
breathlessly silent, and with a great 
flourish brought his hands down on 
the keys. Not a sound ensued! The 
audience tittered. 

Greatly flustered, the performer 
pulled out another stop, then another, 
jiggled one here and another there, 
again made his dramatic pause, and 
again brought his hands down on the 
keys. Not even a sigh came from the 
mighty pipes. .And the audience broke 
into an unrestrained laughter. 

The organist’s suspicions were ar¬ 
oused. Quietly he slipped from his 
bench and made his way to the post 
of the organ pumper. He found the 
old fellow tilted back on his chair, 
smoking his pipe. 

The organist grasped the old man’s 
horny hand. “You were right, my 
friend. We did give them a fine con¬ 
cert, didn’t we? Now give us some 
more wind and we will do even better 
on the second part of the programme.” 

And together they did.

EDWARDS GARDENS 

HI. 7-7421 DON MILLS, ONT. 


Reluctantly we deserted him to his 
“holiday”. How the week dragged! 
Every time it rained, we visioned the 
deluge pouring into his tent, through 
the holes in the sides. We wondered 
if the poison ivy had claimed him for 
its own, yet. We hoped his ankle re¬ 
mained swollen so that he would not 
try swimming in that murky lagoon. 

At last the glorious day of his 
homecoming arrived. My husband 
went personally to the Camp, trusting 
that he might locate some of the boy’s 
equipment. Actually, it was easily 
found. The counsellor, it seemed, had 
merely brought his enthusiasm to 
Camp. Everything else he borrowed 
from the boys. 

Home at last! First, out of those 
dirty clothes and into a warm tub. I 
dropped his hard, time stiffened socks 
down the laundry chute and wasn’t 
too surprised at the hollow “clunk” 
that they made as they hit the basket. 
Had he changed his underwear even 
once? Could this be the same jersey 
he started for camp in, ten days ago? 

A bath brush and plenty of good 
soap can do wonders and soon our 
son was recognizable. Ignoring his 
pyjamas, he began hunting for under¬ 
wear, socks, etc. “Dear, you are going 
to bed,” I reminded him. “Sure, sure,” 
he replied, pulling on a jersey, “but 
our counsellors always had us sleep 
in our clothes. It was faster in the 
tnoming.” 

Nine years have passed, and search¬ 
ing about in our assorted memories of 
camping life, I questioned him the 
other day. “Bun, can you think of 
anything, anything at all, that was 
constructive about that camping holi¬ 
day you took, when you were eight?” 

A wide grin appeared on his face. 
“Just tell them that I learned to ad¬ 
just to disaster.”
